title: Giant Retinal Tear (GRT): Mastery & Management
summary: A Giant Retinal Tear (GRT) is a full-thickness circumferential break extending ≥ 90° (3 clock hours) in the presence of a posterior vitreous detachment. It represents one of the most challenging vitreoretinal surgical frontiers due to the high risk of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and the tendency for the posterior flap to invert.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: A Giant Retinal Tear is defined as a circumferential retinal break involving 90 degrees (three clock hours) or more of the retina. Unlike a retinal dialysis, a GRT occurs at the posterior border of the vitreous base and is associated with a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), leading to the characteristic 'inverted' posterior flap.

branches: High Myopia (Increased axial length & lattice degeneration)

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Mechanism
content: 1. Syneresis and liquefaction of the central vitreous gel.
2. Dynamic traction at the posterior edge of the vitreous base.
3. Rapid circumferential extension of the retinal break.
4. Vitreous enters the subretinal space via the large opening.
5. Gravitational forces and eye movements cause the posterior flap to fold over ('Inversion').

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Sudden onset of persistent Photopsia (flashing lights).
Shower of 'Tobacco Dust' floaters (Shafer's sign / RPE cells).
Peripheral field defect 'Curtain' or 'Shadow'.
Rapid, profound drop in Central Visual Acuity if Macula-off.
Hypotony (Lowered IOP) due to uveoscleral outflow through the tear.

sections.title: The 5 Red Flags of GRT
content: Shafer's Sign (Pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous).
Presence of 'White-Without-Pressure' in the fellow eye.
A flap that crosses the midline (folded over optic nerve).
Rapidly progressive Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR).
History of Stickler Syndrome (Mid-facial hypoplasia/cleft palate).

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Exam Findings
content: Scleral Depression: Mandatory to identify the ends of the tear.
Gonioscopy: To check for RPE cells in the angle and trabecular trauma.
B-Scan Ultrasonography: Essential if media is opaque; shows 'thickened' retina and flap.
Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: 'Inverted' flap showing the RPE side (pale appearance).
Vitreous Base: Look for condensation and 'heavy' traction at the edges.

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: 1. Pre-op: Careful assessment of the fellow eye (360° laser prophylaxis if needed).
2. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): 23g, 25g, or 27g small-gauge approach.
3. Induce PVD & Shave the Vitreous Base: Crucial to remove all traction from the edges.
4. PFCL Injection: Use Perfluorocarbon Liquid to flatten the posterior flap and express subretinal fluid.
5. Endolaser: Apply 3-4 rows of laser to the edge of the tear and 360° to the periphery.
6. Tamponade: Direct PFCL-to-Gas (SF6/C3F8) or PFCL-to-Silicone Oil exchange.
7. Post-operative Positioning: Critical for 1-2 weeks to ensure adhesion.

rows: Wrinkling of inner retinal surface; rolled edges.

sections.title: Surgical Pearls & Technical Nuances
content: Lensectomy: Consider lensectomy to allow aggressive vitreous base shaving and prevent future cataract/oil issues.
PFCL Level: Do not overfill; leave space to work on the retinal edges.
Scleral Buckle: Controversial in GRT; most surgeons avoid unless there is significant anterior PVR.
Edge Trimming: If the flap is very fibrotic or stiff, consider judicious peripheral retinectomy.
Fellow Eye: Up to 50% risk of retinal break/RD in fellow eye in idiopathic cases; 360° laser is standard.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Valved Cannulas: Reduced IOP fluctuations during surgery minimize 'flap flap'.
Heavier-than-water Silicone Oil (Densiron): Useful for inferior GRTs to provide better support.
EVRS Study: Suggested that for GRT without PVR, PPV alone has higher success than buckle/PPV combo.
Digital Visualization (Ngenuity/Artevo): Enhanced depth of field for base shaving.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: PVR (40-50%): The most common cause of surgical failure.
Retinal Slippage: Flap moves during fluid-air exchange (minimised by PFCL-Oil exchange).
Raised IOP: Secondary to silicone oil emulsification or steroid response.
Prognosis: Anatomical success 80-90% with modern techniques, but functional vision varies by macula status.
